Who bills Detroit property tax

Detroit bills its own property tax through the Office of the Treasury. The Office of the Assessor sets the values. Use the due dates printed on your Detroit bill, and call the Office of the Treasury if a date is unclear.

Once a bill is still open after the end of February, it turns delinquent on March 1. From that day only the Wayne County Treasurer accepts payment. Detroit joined the county's Delinquent Tax Revolving Fund program with tax year 2003, under Public Act 246.

What happens when Detroit property tax goes unpaid?

A Detroit parcel can go from delinquent to foreclosed in about two years, and the interest climbs at each step. Here is the sequence the Wayne County Treasurer follows.

Delinquent tax stages for Detroit parcels
StageTimingWhat changes
DelinquentMarch 1 after the tax yearPayable only to Wayne County; interest at 1% a month
ForfeitedThe next March 1Interest becomes 1.5% a month, back to the original delinquency date, plus a $175 foreclosure fee and $30 in recording fees
ForeclosedMarch 31 after a year in forfeiture, in an uncontested caseTitle goes to the Wayne County Treasurer and a judgment is recorded
AuctionSeptember and October of that yearMinimum bid equals taxes, penalties, interest and costs

The office sends at least ten written notices before foreclosure: four during the first year of delinquency and six after forfeiture. A foreclosed parcel is first offered to the state, the city, the county or an authority at the minimum bid. Anything left goes to the September and October auctions, where winning bidders receive a quit claim deed. The county can't waive penalties and interest on a current bill.

Help for owners behind on tax

Wayne County runs payment plans for owners who live in their homes and face financial hardship. The county's income standard is 125% of the federal guideline, and applicants with income just above that line are told to apply anyway. Staff review the file and reply within 30 days of receiving it.

  • Applicants need a Michigan driver's license or state ID, a copy of the deed, proof that the home is the principal residence, and proof of income.
  • Owners by recorded deed or land contract can qualify.
  • The low-income exemption comes from the local assessing unit, so Detroit residents ask the city's assessor, not the county.
  • The treasurer's taxpayer assistance line is (313) 224-5990, and email goes to taxinfo@waynecountymi.gov.
  • The same office can send text reminders about plan payments. Request them by phone or email.
  • A hardship extension that was granted and paid off in an earlier year does not bar a new application if hardship continues.

When the owner has died and the house is still in a relative's name, the treasurer points families to Lakeshore Legal Aid at 888-783-8190 and the Wayne County Probate Court at 313-224-5706. For title help, the county lists United Community Housing Coalition at (313) 963-3310 and Legal Aid and Defender at (313) 964-4130.

Payment plans and a sale

If you cannot pay in full before listing, the payment plan described above is worth asking about early, because staff take up to 30 days to answer. Owners who inherited a house and still have a relative's name on the deed should start with the legal aid and probate court numbers listed in that section, since a deed that is not in your name will slow any sale.

How to appeal a Detroit assessment

Appeals start with the city's Board of Review and can continue to the Michigan Tax Tribunal. Those two bodies can change a tax figure. The Wayne County Treasurer cannot reduce a bill once it is issued.

Call the Office of the Assessor for the current filing window and forms, because the dates change by year. Gather any recent sale prices or repair estimates for your own block before you call, since the board looks at your parcel and not the city as a whole.

Detroit housing at a glance

Detroit has an estimated 649,095 people as of July 2025, a gain of 1.5% since the 2020 census base. Owners occupy 50.3% of housing, across 257,998 households. Owner-held houses carry a median value of $83,900 for 2020-2024, and renters pay a median of $1,074 a month.

Neighborhoods vary a great deal. Downtown, Midtown, Corktown and New Center are dense and historic, and southwest Detroit has seen new housing and business openings. Parts of the northeast and the city's fringes have large numbers of vacant lots. Because the city is so large, one price is a poor guide. Compare your own block.

Where values run this low, an overdue balance of a few thousand dollars can take a big bite out of a sale price. Request the exact payoff early.

Selling with taxes owed

Under MCL 211.135 a register of deeds asks for treasurer certificates covering tax liens and a five-year tax history before a deed is recorded. A warranty deed can be refused until they are in the file. Quitclaim deeds and some other conveyances are excepted.

Deed certification happens at Wayne County's Treasurer's Office, 400 Monroe Street, 5th Floor, Detroit, MI 48226, for $5 a document with up to 25 parcel numbers and 20 cents for each parcel beyond that. Only originals qualify, never copies. The certified deed then moves on to the county's recording office, which needs its own appointment.

At a closing, the title company pays the tax balance out of your proceeds and relies on the treasurer's certification. Ask the county for a written payoff first, because interest keeps adding up each month. A cash sale can skip the lender's timeline, but the tax balance still has to clear before the deed is recorded.

A practical order of steps when you plan to sell with a balance due:

  1. Find out whether the bill is still with the city or has turned delinquent and moved to Wayne County.
  2. Ask the right office for a written payoff figure, and ask again close to the closing date, since interest is added each month.
  3. Give your title company the payoff so it can order the treasurer certification for the deed.
  4. Bring the original deed, never a copy, if you handle certification yourself at the Treasurer's Office.
  5. Book the county recording appointment once the certified deed is back in your hands.

Delinquent payments by bank transfer online cost nothing, while cards add 2.49%, which goes to the service provider. Wayne County warns that its staff never come to a home to collect money, so pay only at the office, online, at an authorized kiosk or by mail.

Frequently asked questions

Who takes payment on delinquent Detroit property tax?

The Wayne County Treasurer. Unpaid bills turn delinquent on March 1 and are payable only to the county from then on. The office is at 400 Monroe Street, 5th Floor, Detroit, and takes calls at (313) 224-5990.

How fast can Detroit tax foreclosure happen?

Roughly two years. A parcel forfeits on the March 1 after delinquency begins, then can be foreclosed the following March 31 in an uncontested case, with auctions in September and October.

What interest applies to delinquent Detroit property tax?

Interest runs 1% a month at first, then 1.5% a month once the parcel is forfeited, applied back to the date the tax became delinquent. A $175 fee and $30 recording fee are added at forfeiture.

Can a Detroit house with back taxes be sold?

Yes. Proceeds cover the balance at the closing table, and the title company relies on the treasurer's certification. Ask Wayne County for a written payoff first, because interest keeps adding up.

Does Detroit offer relief from property tax?

Possibly. Wayne County runs payment plans for owner-occupants, and the low-income exemption is requested through the city's assessing office. Ask the Office of the Assessor for the current application.

Who bills and collects property tax in Ann Arbor

Ann Arbor collects its own property tax through the city Treasury unit, and the city Assessor sets the values behind each bill. If real property tax stays unpaid past winter, the account moves to Washtenaw County.

Property tax is more than half of the city's revenue, so assessments get close attention. Your bill is a combined figure: the city levy plus the county, the schools and other taxing units, each with its own millage.

A separate administration fee also appears. State law lets the city add up to 1 percent of the tax, and the money offsets the cost of defending assessments and collecting for every taxing unit.

Due dates and penalties

Two bills arrive each year. Summer tax is billed July 1 and winter tax December 1, and the last penalty-free days fall at the end of those months. County operating tax rides on the summer bill, and the voted county millages ride on the winter one.

Missing the winter deadline starts a short countdown. Real property tax still unpaid on February 28 goes to the Washtenaw County Treasurer, and extra penalties and interest begin March 1. After that handoff the city can no longer show the account, so call the county to find out whether a late balance has been paid.

Ann Arbor tax dates and ways to pay
Payment or deadlineWhen or where
Summer taxPayable from July 1, due July 31
Winter taxPayable from December 1, due December 31

How the tax is calculated

The formula is simple. Take the taxable value, divide by 1,000, multiply by the millage rate, then multiply by 1.01 for the fee. Taxable value often trails assessed value because Proposal A, passed by Michigan voters in 1994, ties its yearly growth to the smaller of 5 percent or inflation, with additions counted separately. Assessed value itself targets half of market value.

The city's online estimator shows annual millage totals of 52.8802 for principal residences and 68.8196 for other property. Rates change from year to year, and your parcel's actual bill depends on the units that cover it.

Your taxable value is printed on the annual bill and on the assessment notice, which the city mails around the first week of March. The online property record card holds the figures behind both.

Why the bill jumps after a sale

After a sale or transfer, the next tax year's taxable value is set equal to the assessed value, the half-of-market figure. Ann Arbor calls that uncapping. The yearly limit then applies again until ownership changes once more.

That rule is why a buyer's first full bill can top the one you paid. A long-held house may carry a taxable value well under its assessed value, and the buyer starts without that cushion. With homes valued at a median of $453,400, the difference can be sizable. Buyers often ask about it, so expect the question at showings.

The Assessor's Office, on the fifth floor of Larcom City Hall, takes the Property Transfer Affidavit, the Principal Residence Exemption affidavit and the request to rescind that exemption. Hand them in, submit them on the online forms page or mail them. Questions go to 734.794.6530 or assessor@a2gov.org.

How to appeal your assessment

Start with the city Board of Review, which sits four days beginning the Monday of March's third week. You appear by appointment, and the Assessor hands out the appeal forms. Board members are appointed citizens, approved by council, and do not work for the city.

The case that works shows assessed value running past 50 percent of true cash value. Complaining that taxes keep climbing does not count, because taxable value may rise yearly by inflation or 5 percent, whichever is lower. Useful evidence includes comparable nearby sales, mistakes on your record card and a repair estimate for something like a leaking basement.

  • A homeowner has to protest at the local board before taking a case to the Michigan Tax Tribunal.
  • The Tribunal filing date is July 31 for homes, and May 31 for commercial and industrial real property and business personal property.
  • The board mails its decision some weeks after it adjourns, along with the next appeal steps.

Deferment and delinquent balances

Certain owners can put off the summer bill: senior citizens, people with qualifying disabilities or blindness, and eligible service members and their surviving spouses. A summer deferment carries a $40,000 household income cap. Pick up the application at the Customer Service Center, 301 E. Huron St., or find it at washtenaw.org, and file it with the treasurer by September 15.

Real property balances that moved to the county are handled by the Washtenaw County Treasurer at 734.222.6600 or taxes@washtenaw.org. Overdue personal property tax stays with the city, and 734.994.2833 gives the amount.

Selling with taxes owed

If you plan to sell with a bill outstanding, request the figures before you list. The closing agent pays what is owed from your proceeds, so a clear number early keeps the settlement statement from surprising you. Ask for the figure in writing if you can, and note which taxing unit holds the balance, since the city and the county answer for different accounts.

A practical order of steps: ask the city Treasury for the current balance, and the county if anything went past February 28. Gather your Property Transfer Affidavit and, if it applies, the request to rescind your Principal Residence Exemption. Then give the closing agent both numbers so the payoff is built into the closing.

A cash sale does not change what the tax bill says, but it can skip the repair negotiations and lender appraisal that slow a conventional closing.

Ann Arbor housing at a glance

The estimated 2025 population is 122,233. Owners hold 45.5 percent of 50,499 households, so renters are the majority, and many sellers here are landlords or heirs with an older house. The typical home value is $453,400 and typical gross rent is $1,649. Monthly owner costs at the midpoint run $2,436 with a mortgage and $1,036 without. When repairs stand in the way of a conventional sale, a buyer who takes the property as-is can close without them.

Frequently asked questions

What is the due date for Ann Arbor summer tax?

July 31, with payments accepted from July 1. Winter tax runs on the same pattern, opening December 1 and closing December 31.

Where can I pay my Ann Arbor tax in person?

Use the Customer Service and Payment Center inside Larcom City Hall, 301 E. Huron St., open weekdays 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. A drive-up drop box at East Ann Street and North Fifth Avenue stays open around the clock.

Does selling change an Ann Arbor taxable value?

Yes, for the buyer. The year after a transfer, taxable value is reset to the assessed value, a step the city calls uncapping.

When must an Ann Arbor homeowner file with the Michigan Tax Tribunal?

By July 31, after first protesting at the March Board of Review. Commercial and industrial real property and business personal property must file by May 31.

Who collects Ann Arbor real property tax that is still unpaid in March?

The Washtenaw County Treasurer, at 734.222.6600, takes real property tax not received by February 28. Delinquent personal property tax stays with the city.

Who sends and who values the bill

Three offices touch a Sterling Heights bill. The Office of Treasury at 40555 Utica Road sends and collects current-year tax, with counter hours of 8:30 to 5:00 on weekdays. The Assessing Office sets values and logs ownership changes. Macomb County takes over any balance still open on March 1.

Tell the right desk when something changes. A new lender means a call to Treasury at 586-446-2780. A transfer of ownership or a principal residence update goes to Assessing at 586-446-2340. If your tax is escrowed, you get a marked courtesy copy and the original goes to the escrow agent.

Each parcel gets two bills a year from the City Treasurer's Office, one in summer and one in winter.

If you are selling, a handy order of calls is Treasury first for what is owed, then Assessing for the exemption and transfer paperwork. Have the parcel ID in front of you for both calls, and write down the date and the name of the person who gave you each figure so the title company can match it later.

Due dates and late charges

Summer tax can be paid without penalty from July 1 until the first business day of September. The winter window runs from December 1 to the last day of February. Summer bills go out in late June and winter bills in late November.

Sterling Heights bill schedule and late charges
BillMailedPayable without penaltyIf left unpaid
SummerLate JuneJuly 1 through the first business day in SeptemberOne-half of 1% per month after September 1 through the end of February
WinterLate NovemberDecember 1 through the end of FebruaryOn March 1, an added 3% interest, then transfer to Macomb County

Whatever remains on either bill on March 1 follows that path. From then on, and for any earlier-year bill, you pay at the Macomb County Building in Mount Clemens (phone 586-469-5190), where further penalties accrue.

How to pay

Pick a method based on how close the deadline is. A reply envelope comes with the bill, and the city adds drop boxes, a card line and eCheck.

  • Mail a check made out to City of Sterling Heights in the supplied envelope, which is addressed to a Chicago post office box, with the parcel ID on the check.
  • Drop it in a secured box on the city center campus, either by the Police Department entrance or by the Utica entrance to City Hall.
  • Use a card at 877-495-2729 or on the payment website. Point and Pay adds a convenience fee, and American Express is declined.
  • Draw on a checking or savings account through the eCheck choice on that website.

Water and sewer bills can end up on the tax roll too. Delinquent utility accounts are transferred to the tax rolls twice a year after City Manager approval. If you have a past-due utility account, settle it before closing so it never lands on a tax bill.

How a sale changes taxable value

Assessing works out assessed value, half of true cash value, from a two-year sales study. Voters passed Proposal A on March 15, 1994, which added taxable value: the smaller of state equalized value and a capped value. The cap is the prior year's taxable value grown by inflation or 5%, whichever is lower, plus construction changes.

A transfer releases the cap. The next year, taxable value jumps to state equalized value with no ceiling, so your old bill can sit far below the first bill the buyer sees. The price on one deed does not set the new value, because the city adjusts land and building values citywide from the study period and avoids reassessing from a single transaction.

Long-time owners should warn buyers about that first bill. Filing falls to the buyer: Property Transfer Affidavit form 2766, delivered to Assessing inside 45 days.

Appeals and the Principal Residence Exemption

The yearly Notice of Assessment, Taxable Valuation, and Property Classification normally goes out on the final day of February. March Board of Review sessions usually open the third Monday of the month, with two panels of three city residents hearing appeals on value, classification and hardship. Written answers reach appellants by the first Monday in June. An unhappy residential owner can then petition the Michigan Tax Tribunal.

  • Principal Residence Exemption: if the notice shows 0%, file form 2368 with Assessing by June 1 to affect the summer levy or by November 1 to affect the winter levy.
  • Rescission: an owner who stops living in the house must file form 2602 to end the exemption.
  • Tax information lookup: the city posts an online property tax lookup for any parcel.

Selling a home in Sterling Heights

Sterling Heights is a second-ring suburb in Macomb County, 14 to 20 miles north of downtown Detroit. Two freeways frame the city, M-53 (Van Dyke) and M-59 (Hall Road), with Mound Road running north and south. Two school districts split it: Utica Community Schools covers the northern half and Warren Consolidated Schools covers the southern half. Buyers ask about the district first, so know which one serves your street.

The city has 133,931 people in 51,736 households. Three in four homes (75.8%) are owner-occupied, with a median value of $274,300 and median gross rent of $1,292. Owners with a mortgage report median monthly costs of $1,681, and those without report $666. Ask Assessing for numbers on your own parcel, since a citywide median says little about one street.

Winters are cold, with 39.1 days a year when the temperature stays below freezing. Buyers tend to look hard at roofs and basements, so have repair receipts ready.

Steps before closing

Order a tax status from Treasury so the title company knows what is owed on each bill. Pay any past-due water or sewer balance first. If you claimed the Principal Residence Exemption, send Assessing form 2602 once you move out.

The buyer files form 2766 within 45 days and, if moving in, form 2368 by the June 1 or November 1 deadline. Blank copies are available at Assessing and on the city and state Treasury websites. A cash buyer follows the same filing rules, and a quick closing still needs the payoff figure from Treasury in hand, so request it as soon as you have an offer.

Frequently asked questions

What is the last day to pay Sterling Heights summer tax without a penalty?

The last day is the first business day in September. After September 1, the city adds one-half of 1% per month through the end of February.

Where does my Sterling Heights tax go if I miss the February deadline?

It goes to Macomb County. On March 1 the city adds 3% interest and transfers any balance on a summer or winter bill. Payment is then made at the Macomb County Building, 1 South Main, Mount Clemens, at 586-469-5190.

Who files the transfer affidavit after a Sterling Heights sale?

The buyer does. Form 2766 goes to the Assessing Office inside 45 days, and blank copies are at the office and on the city and state Treasury websites.

How do I end the exemption after moving out of a Sterling Heights house?

Send the Assessing Office a Request to Rescind Homeowner's Principal Residence Exemption, form 2602. A buyer moving in files form 2368, with deadlines of June 1 for the summer levy and November 1 for the winter.

Can I pay Sterling Heights property tax by phone?

Yes. Call 877-495-2729 to pay by card, and expect a convenience fee from Point and Pay. American Express is not accepted. The payment website also takes eCheck payments from a checking or savings account.

Only in March. The Notice of Assessment arrives at the end of February, headed with a line saying it is no tax bill, and it lists the board's meeting dates.

Once the March Board of Review adjourns, the city's assessors have no legal power to alter the number. Commercial and industrial owners may skip the board and petition the Michigan Tax Tribunal by May 31. For homes, state law sets July 31 of the tax year as the tribunal deadline, after a protest at the board. The city has at times accepted notarized letters, with original signatures and supporting papers, in place of a visit, so ask the assessor what the coming year allows.

  • Hardship relief: the online services page lists a low-income hardship application called HOPE.
  • Disabled veteran owners: file an affidavit with the assessor along with the explanation of benefits.
  • Principal residence exemption: the owner must live in the home by June 1. It lifts 18 mills of school operating tax. Tell the city when you move out, because skipping that step can bring a denial with penalties.

Flint due dates

The dates printed on your Flint bill rule, since the city bills on its own calendar. If no bill reached you, contact the city.

Behind the city's calendar sit two state rules. The summer levy attaches to the property on July 1, and summer tax collected with city taxes takes the same penalties as the city's other charges. Any balance left on March 1 is handed to the county treasurer as delinquent, at which point a 4% county fee and interest of 1% a month begin.

Where an unpaid Flint bill ends up

At the county, and after about three years the parcel can be foreclosed and auctioned. Here is Michigan's schedule for county foreclosing units.

  • Year one, March 1: the unpaid bill is returned to the county and the 4% fee and monthly interest start to build.
  • Year two, March 1: the parcel forfeits, a $175 title fee goes on, and redemption carries half a percent a month counted from the prior March 1.
  • Year three, March 30 and 31: the circuit court must enter its judgment by the 30th, and the 31st is the final day to redeem before title moves to the county.
  • After that: public agencies get a first chance to buy, then online auctions run. Genesee County holds several rounds each fall.

A former owner whose house sold at auction for more than the taxes and costs may be able to claim the surplus. Ask the Genesee County Treasurer what the claim process requires.

Selling a Flint house that owes tax

You can. The title company requests a payoff from the city or county, adds interest and fees through the closing date, and subtracts the total from your proceeds.

The seller also owes transfer tax: $3.75 per $500 of price to the state, plus 55 cents per $500 to the county, which applies to any Michigan county under two million residents, Genesee included. Both go to the county treasurer within 15 days of delivering the deed. Foreclosure transfers, deeds to a child or grandchild and land contracts that keep title with the seller are among the listed exemptions.

Two city filings follow a sale. File a property transfer affidavit with the assessor, and if you took the principal residence exemption, file a rescission. When back taxes, repairs or a tenant make a listing slow, a cash purchase as-is lets the payoff come out in one step at the table.

A simple order of work for an owner with a balance:

  1. Find out whether the bill is with the city or has moved to Genesee County.
  2. Request a payoff that runs to your expected closing date.
  3. Give it to the title company so it can deduct the amount from your proceeds.
  4. After closing, file the transfer affidavit and the exemption rescission with the assessor.

Who gets my payment on a current Flint tax bill?

The City of Flint takes it, online through InvoiceCloud or by the methods on the bill. After a balance moves to the county on March 1, you pay the Genesee County Treasurer at 324 S Saginaw St Ste 2A instead.

Is a residential assessment open to challenge after March?

No. Flint's value becomes final when the March Board of Review closes. Commercial and industrial owners are the exception and can petition the Michigan Tax Tribunal directly by May 31.

Why did my Flint taxes jump after a purchase?

Taxable value resets to assessed value in the year after a sale, which can raise the bill sharply. The assessor suggests calling your lender if the tax is escrowed, since the payment may need to change.

Does a Flint buyer take on my unpaid tax?

The tax is a lien on the parcel under state law, so it must be cleared for the buyer to get clean title. A title company usually pays it out of the seller's proceeds at closing.

Who writes the transfer tax check on a Flint sale?

The seller does. Michigan sets $3.75 per $500 for the state and 55 cents per $500 for the county, and the money goes to the county treasurer within 15 days of the deed's delivery.

The Assessing Department prepares the roll and tracks 59,077 parcels, roughly 54,620 real and 4,457 personal. The Treasurer's Office mails the bills and acts as collection agent for every unit levying inside the city: Warren itself, the county and the millages of six school districts.

They are delinquent and must be paid to the Macomb County Treasurer. The county adds the city's collection fees, an additional 4 percent fee, and 1 percent interest for every month the balance stays open.

Only the March Board of Review can change an opinion of value on a house. A residential owner must protest there before moving on to the Michigan Tax Tribunal. Warren is a 34-square-mile grid between 8 Mile and 14 Mile roads, bordering Detroit on its south side, with Center Line entirely enclosed inside it. I-696, M-53 (Van Dyke), M-97 and Mound Road carry most traffic. Southeast Warren, including Warrendale, Berkshire Manor and Belangers Garden, has many bungalows from just after World War II, with brick ranches north of Stephens Road built after 1960.

August 31. The summer bill may be paid whole or in two parts, with part two billed December 1 and due January 31. After August 31 the entire summer balance is required.

To the Macomb County Treasurer. The city stops accepting it after the last day of February, and the county adds the city's fees, a 4 percent fee and 1 percent monthly interest.

Is online filing allowed for a Warren assessment appeal?

No. Appeals are accepted in person by appointment or by letter received before the deadline. Residential owners must go through the March Board of Review before the Michigan Tax Tribunal.

Will a Warren tax bill change after the house sells?

Yes. The next year the buyer's taxable value is set equal to the assessed value, which is half of market value. That can sit far above the capped figure the seller paid.

Primary-residence owners earning $40,000 or less who are 62 or older or fall into a listed veteran, widow, blind or disabled group. The form is due September 15 and moves the due date to February 14.

The summer bill is due July 31 and the winter bill February 14, each shifting to the following business day when it lands on a weekend. Whatever date applies is printed on your bill.

How taxable value becomes a bill

Everything starts with taxable value, the number the city taxes, which may equal or fall below assessed value. The assessor revisits market value yearly to set both.

How to dispute a Grand Rapids value

Start in February at the Assessor's Review by filing a petition with the City Assessor. Unhappy with the answer? Appeal in March to the Board of Review, in writing or by appointment. Only owners who already petitioned the assessor may appear in March.

The July and December boards are narrower. They fix qualified errors the assessor has verified for the current and one earlier year, such as a clerical slip, a mutual mistake of fact or a measuring or math error, and they can grant a hardship exemption for the current year alone. MCL 211.53b is the controlling statute.

Waiting for a board does not suspend payment. After the board's final report reaches the treasurer, a corrected bill follows in roughly 30 days, yet the first bill stays due and penalties keep running. Refunds are paid to whoever paid the tax.

Do this early in the year of a purchase, since the exemption is what lowers your school tax. File by June 1 with the City Assessor, using the PRE affidavit. MCL 211.7cc requires a qualified owner who lives in the home as a principal residence and triggers no disqualifying rule.

Missing June 1 can sometimes be repaired. The assessor may ask for proof that the owner lived there on that date and then adjust the current year and as many as three prior years.

Two checkpoints touch a sale. A recorded warranty deed needs a county treasurer certificate under MCL 211.135 covering the five prior years. The title company also wants a written payoff, which the city treasurer provides for current bills and the Kent County Treasurer for anything past March 1.

An owner facing a balance can list on the market, sell as-is to a cash buyer, or pay it down first. Collect written payoff numbers before choosing a closing date. Here is a workable order:

  1. Check whether the bill sits with the city or has moved to the county.
  2. Call the right treasurer for a written payoff.
  3. Hand the payoff to the title company and ask it to order the county certificate.
  4. If you took the PRE, tell the assessor after the sale so the next bill goes to the buyer correctly.

A cash sale as-is skips the lender's timeline, but the payoff and the certificate are still required.

Grand Rapids housing and rental parcels

Grand Rapids has 80,222 households, a median owner-occupied value of $244,500 and an owner-occupancy rate of 54.0%. Median gross rent is $1,266 and median household income is $69,108.

With nearly half of homes rented, owners of rental parcels should remember that the PRE reaches only the part of a property the owner lives in. The city's Economic Development Department also runs incentive programs for vacant or obsolete property and answers at 616-456-3431.

What day is the Grand Rapids summer tax due?

July 31, or the next business day when that is a weekend. Bills go out in the first week of July, and a 1% charge builds for each month the balance sits unpaid.

The Kent County Treasurer. Unpaid real property bills leave the city on that date, and the county adds penalties and a 4% administrative fee.

June 1, filed with the City Assessor. A late filing may still be accepted with proof of owner occupancy on that date, reaching the current year and up to three earlier ones.

No. The original bill stays due. If the board changes the value, the treasurer revises the bill within about 30 days of the final report, and refunds go to whoever paid.

Who bills and collects property tax in Livonia?

The City of Livonia assesses and bills its own property tax, and Wayne County steps in only after a bill goes delinquent. The Assessment Department sets values and handles exemption forms. The Treasurer's Office, on the first floor of City Hall at 33000 Civic Center Drive, mails real and personal property tax bills on July 1 and December 1 and collects the payments.

Those payments are split among several taxing bodies: the City of Livonia, Livonia Public Schools, Clarenceville Public Schools, Schoolcraft College, the State of Michigan education tax, Wayne County, Wayne County RESA and Oakland ISD. A house in the northeast corner of the city that falls in the Clarenceville district carries a different mix of levies than one in the Livonia Public Schools territory.

Due dates and penalties

Summer taxes are billed July 1 and due September 14. Winter taxes are billed December 1 and due February 14. When a due date falls on a weekend or holiday, the due date moves to the next business day. Checks go to City of Livonia, Treasurer, 33000 Civic Center Drive, Livonia, MI 48154.

Delinquent personal property tax stays with the city treasurer, while delinquent real property tax moves to the county.

Looking up a tax bill and special assessments

The city runs an online property inquiry system at livoniatax.org, using BS&A software. Agree to the disclaimer, search by address, and enter only the street name without Road, Street or Avenue, or just the house number. Click the property, open the Tax Information tab, and the taxes appear by year and season, with a detailed breakdown behind each year.

Errors on the site do not cancel taxes or special assessments owed. The official records at City Hall cover current-year collections only, and payments on delinquent taxes do not appear online. To check a delinquent balance, contact the Wayne County Treasurer.

Special assessments are a separate item. Email specials@livonia.gov to request the status on a parcel. Vacant and abandoned property fees, permit issues and violations are missing from the online system, so a seller who wants a clean closing should ask Inspection for those directly.

Print or save the page for the year you need. Lenders and title companies often ask for proof that both seasons are paid, and the Tax Information tab shows each season separately, which makes the answer easy to hand over.

Exemptions and deferrals

An affidavit for the principal residence exemption filed on or before June 1 earns the exemption on that year's summer and winter levy and later years while the home remains the owner's principal residence. One filed after June 1 and on or before November 1 applies to the current winter levy and later levies.

The city also publishes a form letting a homeowner defer the due date of winter taxes on a principal residence without penalty or interest, for a stated period set each year. Ask the Treasurer's Office which year's form and deadline applies. Hardship exemptions run through the local assessing unit, so Livonia owners in a tight spot should start with the Assessment Department, not the county.

Religious, charitable and educational exemption forms, plus personal property forms, are on the Assessment Department page, which accepts forms by email, mail or the City Hall drop box on the east side of the building.

Mark both dates on a calendar if you recently bought. A buyer who closes in the spring and files after June 1 still gets the exemption for the winter levy, so a late filing is worth making rather than skipping.

If Livonia property taxes go unpaid

Unpaid summer and winter bills are forwarded to the Wayne County Treasurer. On March 1 unpaid taxes become delinquent at the county, adding a 4 percent administration fee and 1 percent interest per month. A $15 collection fee follows on October 1. The next March 1 the parcel forfeits to the county treasurer, with a $175 fee and recording fees, and interest rises to 1.5 percent per month retroactive to the first delinquency.

Foreclosure follows. Michigan's three-year process ends with the circuit court entering a judgment, and unpaid taxes on March 31 of the third year mean the owner loses the property. Wayne County sends at least ten notices before that point.

Owners with a financial hardship can apply for a Wayne County payment plan. The income limit is 125 percent of the federal level, and the application needs photo ID, a copy of the deed, proof of occupancy and proof of income. After a foreclosure, the former owner can claim remaining auction proceeds by filing a notice of intent by July 1 of that year.

Selling with taxes owed

Livonia is a Wayne County city of about 95,500 people at the 2020 census, with more than 40,000 housing units and only 2.7 percent of them vacant. Many homes here have been owned for decades, so a long-held house often has a taxable value well below its market value, a gap that closes for the next owner after a sale.

Most Livonia homes sold with tax due close like any other. The title company gets a payoff, pays the city or county from the seller's proceeds, and records the deed. Work through it in this order:

  • Pull the current bill at livoniatax.org and note the season and amount.
  • Ask the Treasurer's Office at (734) 466-2245 whether the bill is still with the city.
  • If the bill is delinquent, ask Wayne County for the payoff figure, since City Hall no longer holds the balance.
  • Email specials@livonia.gov for special assessments and call Inspection at (734) 466-2580 for open permits or violations.

September 14. The summer bill is mailed July 1, and if September 14 lands on a weekend or holiday the due date becomes the next business day.

Where do I pay Livonia winter taxes?

Mail a check payable to the City of Livonia to Treasurer, 33000 Civic Center Drive, Livonia, MI 48154, or use the Treasurer's Office on the first floor of City Hall. Winter bills are due February 14.

Who do I call about a delinquent Livonia tax bill?

The Wayne County Treasurer. Delinquent real property taxes are turned over to the county, and the city's own records show current-year collections only.

How do I get the principal residence exemption in Livonia?

File the affidavit with the Assessment Department. Filing by June 1 covers that year's summer and winter taxes, and filing after June 1 through November 1 covers the winter levy.

Which school districts tax Livonia homes?

Livonia Public Schools serves most of the city, and a portion of the northeast is in Clarenceville Public Schools. Both appear among the bodies that receive the city's collections.

Who handles your Kalamazoo tax bill

The city splits the work. The Assessor sets values and the Treasurer sends bills. The assessor's counter is at City Hall, 241 W South Street, open Monday through Friday from 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Call (269) 337-8000 or email assessor@kalamazoocity.org. Two drop boxes take payments and paperwork around the clock: one at the front of City Hall and a drive-up box on St. Johns Place at West Lovell Street.

When the local collection window closes, the Kalamazoo County Treasurer takes over any unpaid balance. Sellers get caught at that handoff, because the county adds heavier charges than the city does.

Kalamazoo is the county seat, with 73,598 people at the 2020 census and 72,683 residents in mid 2025. Renters outnumber owners here: owners live in only 42.3 percent of homes. The middle home value is $179,000 and median gross rent is $1,078 a month. Rentals, inherited houses and homes with deferred repairs often reach a sale with tax balances attached, so check your parcel on the city's BS&A Online lookup before you list. It shows tax history, payment dates, amounts due and permit history.

Due dates and payment options

Each year's tax comes as two bills. Summer notices go out by July 1 and are due July 31, either in one payment or as six monthly installments that stay interest free while on time. Winter notices go out by December 1 and are due the following February 14, in one payment.

Kalamazoo city property tax calendar

By December 1Winter bills mailed

The payment processor charges card users 2.8 percent with a $1.50 minimum, and electronic check users $0.85. Those fees apply online, by phone or in person.

Late bills at the county

Once the County Treasurer takes over a delinquent balance, it carries a 4 percent administrative fee and monthly interest of 1 percent, plus costs for mailings, recording, title work and site visits. The county's sample schedule for 2025 taxes runs like this:

  • Local payment closes February 28. After that the county collects.
  • A $15 notice charge lands on October 1 of the next year.
  • The next March 1, a parcel more than a year behind is forfeited and picks up half a percent monthly interest, 6 percent retroactive interest and a $175 title search charge.
  • Recording certificates adds $60, an in person site visit $50, and the newspaper listing $50.
  • Foreclosure follows at 25 months, with ownership passing to the County Treasurer on April 1.

Once the county owns the parcel, the owner cannot take it back. A person named on the deed may claim surplus money from an auction sale, and no treasurer can waive penalties or interest.

Deferrals and payment plans

A low income owner can ask to push the summer bill back to the winter due date. Income for the preceding year must be $40,000 or less, and the applicant must be 62 or older, the unmarried surviving spouse of such a person, blind, paraplegic, hemiplegic, quadriplegic, totally and permanently disabled, or an eligible veteran, service member, widow or widower. Applications must reach the City Treasurer's Office by September 15. There is no winter deferral.

Once a bill reaches the county, the Treasurer can set up an extension agreement at an appointment with its foreclosure prevention team. Call 269-384-8124. The county expects two tax years to be cleared each calendar year, and dangerous or condemned buildings are not eligible.

Partial payments to the county are welcome because they slow the monthly interest. Staff there will also check whether you qualify for a home or disability related exemption.

How to appeal your assessment

Start with the March Board of Review. MCL 211.30 sets its opening for the second Monday of March, and the city may pick the Tuesday or Wednesday after. The board sits at least 12 hours that week, including 3 hours after 6 p.m.

If the board agrees the value is off, it adjusts the assessed and taxable amounts. You get written word of the outcome by the first Monday in June, along with notice of your right to appeal further.

The next level is the Michigan Tax Tribunal, an independent tax court. Its Small Claims division hears most residential appeals in informal telephone sessions of about half an hour, and owners often appear without a lawyer. The board's notice gives the last day to file, so check it when it arrives.

Tax certificates when you sell

A warranty deed needs two certificates. In the city, the County Treasurer will not issue one until the City Treasurer has issued one, for $10 at City Hall, 241 W South Street, phone 269-337-8036. The county certificate then costs $5 for up to 20 tax ID numbers. The state rule is MCL 211.135, which looks back five years from the deed date.

At the recording counter, 201 West Kalamazoo Avenue, the seller also owes transfer tax of $1.10 per $1,000 to the county and $7.50 per $1,000 to the state, after rounding the price up to the next $500. The deed itself costs $30 to record.

Tax owed on the house is usually paid out of closing proceeds. Ask the treasurer holding the bill for the payoff, because city and county records are updated separately.

Homestead exemption when you sell

Owners who live in their home can claim the principal residence exemption, which removes a slice of the local school operating tax. You must own and occupy the property by May 1 and file an affidavit with the Assessor.

Selling means new paperwork. The seller rescinds the exemption with the assessor, and the buyer files an affidavit of their own. Someone buying a replacement house can hold the old exemption for up to three years if the old house is vacant, listed, unleased and unused for business. The request is due May 1 following the exemption claim on the new house, and refiling by December 31 each year extends it for up to two more years.

Tell the closing agent when you moved out. A wrong exemption status on a sold house leads to corrected bills later.

Selling with taxes owed

If you owe back taxes, the first step is a payoff figure from whichever treasurer holds the bill: the city before March 1, the county after. Title companies pay these balances from your proceeds at closing, so a delinquent bill does not block a sale, but the extra fees listed above do come out of your pocket.

A seller who is behind and short on time can ask the county's foreclosure prevention team about an extension before listing. A cash sale to a buyer who closes quickly can also stop interest and fees from growing, since the balance is settled at the table.

Frequently asked questions

When is the winter tax bill due in Kalamazoo?

February 14 of the year after billing, paid in full. Anything open on March 1 moves to the Kalamazoo County Treasurer as delinquent.

Can I split the summer bill into installments?

Yes, into six monthly payments, once the first installment arrives by July 31. A late first payment brings a single 3 percent penalty, and interest of 1 percent then accrues each month.

Who decides what my house is assessed at?

The City Assessor's Office does. If you disagree, the March Board of Review hears you first, with the Michigan Tax Tribunal as the next step.

Who can defer a summer bill?

Owners with prior year household income of $40,000 or under who are also 62 or older, blind, totally and permanently disabled, or a qualifying veteran, service member, widow or widower. The City Treasurer must receive the form by September 15.

How much are the tax certificates for a warranty deed?

Ten dollars for the city certificate and five for the county one. A parcel inside the city needs both.

Which Dearborn office sends the tax bill?

The city's own Treasury Division does. Dearborn lies in Wayne County, yet the city sends the bill and takes the payment, at the cashier's counter in the Dearborn Administrative Center, 16901 Michigan Avenue, weekdays from eight to half past four.

Valuation is a separate office. The Assessing Department in Suite 5 of the same building sets every parcel's value yearly, answers at 313-943-2140 and keeps weekday hours of eight to five. Email and voicemail get a reply within 48 hours, and in all cases within seven business days.

Deed copies live elsewhere. The Wayne County Register of Deeds, International Building, 400 Monroe, sixth floor, Detroit, holds them, and owners who need liber and page numbers go there.

Due dates and installments

Two bills arrive each year. The summer levy is struck on July 1 and falls due September 14. The winter levy is struck on December 1 and falls due February 14.

SummerJuly 1September 14, or three installments on Sept. 14, Nov. 14 and Jan. 14School, city and county-allocated operating taxes

Splitting the summer bill into installments costs a single $3 fee, and a deferral application exists for eligible residents. Winter tax has no installment option at all.

A postmark earns nothing. Dearborn books a payment on the day the money arrives, so a check in the mail late is a late payment. The 24-hour drop box in the lot facing the Administrative Center's main doors is the safer route near a deadline.

How to pay

Five routes exist, and they differ in cost.

  • Online through BS&A: free for an owner who registers the parcel, with a 3% fee on cards and $3 on an e-check. A tenant who is not the owner pays $6 to set up an account.
  • The DivDat app and the lobby kiosk: cards carry 3%, while e-checks through the app cost nothing.
  • By mail: write the account and parcel numbers on the check and send it to City of Dearborn, Tax Dept. 3102, P.O. Box 30516, Lansing, MI 48909-8016. Certified mail must instead go to the Administrative Center.
  • Automatic ACH debit: free, and you can cancel any time.
  • In person: the cashier's counter, or the drop box outside.

If a closing lands close to a deadline, have the title company pay out of the seller's proceeds by a method that posts that same day.

Why does a Dearborn sale change the next tax bill?

Because the cap resets. Assessed value is half of estimated market value, and Michigan's formula multiplies taxable value, divided by 1,000, by the millage rate. Since Proposal A passed in 1994, an owner's taxable value can grow each year only by inflation or 5%, whichever is lower.

That limit stops applying in the year after ownership transfers. Taxable value then jumps up to assessed value, so the new owner's first bill may sit far above the seller's old one.

Sellers of long-held homes should know this before they talk price with buyers, since buyers will estimate their bill from the uncapped number. Be ready to explain it when a buyer asks why the tax will change.

Is the assessment notice a tax bill?

No. The yearly Change of Assessment Notice arrives by mail ahead of the March board and only reports movement in assessed and taxable value. The dates, times and places of the March Board of Review are printed on it, so keep it until the hearing season ends.

Two kinds of property get assessed: real property, meaning buildings and land, and personal property, meaning the items a business uses to operate. The assessor weighs building size and location, construction materials, lot size, additions, land improvements and any damage or construction work. A homeowner can also compare a parcel's record against the city's residential assessment database, which is searchable online.

Check the record card for errors such as the wrong number of bathrooms or a finished basement that does not exist. Verifying that the record card is accurate is the first step to take.

How to appeal your assessment or request an exemption

Call the Assessing Department first. Plenty of disputes turn out to be a wrong square footage or a misread fact that staff can fix on the spot. When that fails, file with the March Board of Review, the only yearly window to contest value, and one that covers only the current year.

Bring photos, an appraisal or comparable sales along with the petition. A residential owner unhappy with the result can then petition the Michigan Tax Tribunal, though the March board comes first for houses. Commercial and industrial owners may go straight to the tribunal.

  • Principal Residence Exemption: removes up to 18 mills of local school operating tax when the owner lives in the house.
  • Low-income exemption: relief at 50% of value under MCL 211.7u, with the application and documents due by the final December Board of Review session.
  • Disabled veteran exemption: affidavit Form 5107 goes in between January 1 and December 31, with VA proof; a December 30 postmark counts.

What buyers and sellers file after a Dearborn closing

The assessor expects forms from both sides. The buyer owes a Property Transfer Affidavit within 45 days, and being late costs $5 a day, capped at $200 for a house. It is required even if no deed is ever recorded.

The seller who claimed the principal residence exemption sends Form 2602, a request to rescind it, effective on closing day. A buyer who will live in the house sends Form 2368 to claim the exemption, along with a Name and Address Change form.

Unpaid bills are a separate matter. Call the city treasury and the Wayne County Treasurer for exact payoff figures before closing, including penalties and the point where collection moves from the city to the county. If taxes are owed, the title company normally pays them from the seller's proceeds at closing, so ask for the payoff figure early. The title company can also tell you whether the summer or winter bill is the next one due, which decides how much of the year's tax you owe as the seller.

Dearborn housing at a glance

Dearborn is an inner-ring suburb bordering Detroit, with compact lots in about 24.25 square miles and roughly 105,611 residents. The typical owned home is valued at $218,800, and owners live in 68.4% of occupied homes. Median rent is $1,327, and owners pay a median $1,672 monthly with a mortgage or $764 without. Older homes draw questions about roofs, plumbing and wiring, and the Assessing Department lets owners view record cards during business hours.

Frequently asked questions

What is the Dearborn summer tax deadline?

September 14. The bill can be paid in three installments, on September 14, November 14 and January 14, for a single $3 fee.

Does Dearborn offer installments on winter taxes?

No. The winter bill is levied December 1 and must be paid whole by February 14.

Will the city honor a postmark on a mailed tax check?

No, the payment counts on the day the city receives it. A 24-hour drop box in the Administrative Center lot is the alternative.

Where do I begin if I think my Dearborn assessment is wrong?

With the Assessing Department, then the March Board of Review. A residential owner still unsatisfied can go on to the Michigan Tax Tribunal.

What must a buyer file with the city after closing on a Dearborn house?

A Property Transfer Affidavit within 45 days, plus Form 2368 if the buyer will live there and wants the principal residence exemption.

Who bills, collects and values in Troy

Troy's summer and winter bills come from the City Treasurer's Office in City Hall at 500 W Big Beaver Road, which keeps weekday hours of 8 to 4:30. Troy lies in Oakland County, and the county treasurer picks up whatever the city has not collected by March 1.

One Troy bill funds many bodies. Besides city services, the city collects and passes along tax for seven school districts, the county, the Huron-Clinton Metropolitan Authority, the county's art, zoo and transit authorities, Oakland Schools and the Macomb Intermediate School District. A house's school district shapes the millage, which is why the city posts a Millage Rates page.

The City Assessor's Office covers values. It appraises each parcel, processes splits and combinations, and runs the Principal Residence Exemption and Property Transfer Affidavit programs. Call it at 248-524-3311.

Due dates and late charges

Summer statements are mailed July 1 and winter statements December 1. A deadline that falls on a weekend or city holiday slides forward one business day, as with the 2026 winter bills, which run through February 16, 2027.

Paying a Troy bill

Troy accepts automatic debit, mail, cards, e-checks, bank bill pay and walk-in payment. A check or money order placed in an official drop box before 8 a.m. on the business day following a due date still counts as on time.

  • Automatic debit from checking or savings costs nothing, and for winter you choose February 14 or the last business day of December.
  • Cards cost 3%, with a floor of $1.50 online and $2.00 at the counter. E-checks are free below $10,000 and $10 from $10,000 up.
  • Red and blue Official Drop Boxes stand outside City Hall's east walk-up and west drive-up doors, for checks and money orders only.
  • Walk in with the entire statement. Cash, checks, money orders and cards are all taken.

The city's BS&A lookup prints bills and shows payments once you register, which costs nothing. A cleared check is the best receipt, and the city will mail a paper one if you send a stamped, self-addressed envelope.

Help for owners who cannot pay on time

Qualifying households can defer. A Property Tax Deferment moves the due date on both bills to the following April 30. Household income has to be $40,000 or less, and the owner must be 62 or older, paraplegic, hemiplegic or quadriplegic, totally and permanently disabled or blind, or an eligible service person, veteran, widow or widower.

Apply on Michigan Treasury Form 471, delivered to the Treasurer's Office by September 15 with last year's Homestead Property Tax Credit form attached. Questions go to 248.524.3333. Owners outside those groups avoid the March 1 transfer only by paying the winter bill in full on time.

Troy assessments and market values

Troy's 2026 roll holds 35,732 parcels with assessed value of $10,026,428,690 and taxable value of $7,270,919,530. Those totals are up 5.76% and 4.47% on 2025.

Residential real property makes up 28,149 parcels, with assessed value of $6,866,814,460. The average residential parcel carries an assessed value of $243,945, an estimated average market value of $487,890 and an average taxable value of $174,224. In 2025 the city logged 759 valid single-family sales averaging $530,076, with a low of $120,000 and a high of $1,850,000, plus 245 condominium sales averaging $375,029.

The gap between assessed and taxable value matters when you sell. Assessed value follows the market, while taxable value is capped for as long as one owner holds the home. The next owner's first bill is usually higher than yours.

How do I appeal a Troy assessment?

For a Troy homeowner, the March Board of Review is the single chance to contest a residential value, and a missed session means waiting a year. Mid-February brings a notice of assessment to every property whose assessed value changed, listing protest dates. If it never reaches you, the values still stand.

When city appraisers visit, they carry marked badges and measure the outside of the house and any improvements. Participation is voluntary, and staff do not need to enter the home, although they ask about the interior and mail a survey. General maintenance such as new gutters, a roof or windows is not assessable. What raises value is air conditioning, decks, porches, patios, sheds, additions, garages, finished basements and added bathrooms. Appointments run through the Assessing Department, with field slots between 9:00 a.m. and 2:30 p.m.

The department processed about 2,448 recorded deeds in 2025, and most produced a Property Transfer Affidavit. It handles a similar number of Principal Residence Exemption affidavits each year. Businesses must file personal property statements by February 20.

Selling a home in Troy

Troy covers about 33.5 square miles and sits on Interstate 75. Somerset Collection and Oakland Mall anchor retail, and Amtrak's Wolverine train stops at the Troy Transit Center. Seven districts reach into Troy. Troy School District serves most addresses, with Troy High School and Athens High School as its two zoned high schools. Avondale, Birmingham and Warren Consolidated also run schools inside the city, so confirm the district for any address you are marketing.

The city has 88,733 residents. Nearly three of four homes (73.3%) are owner-occupied, at a median value of $420,300, and median household income is $120,045. Recent sales on your own street will say more than any citywide median.

Before you list, ask the Treasurer for the balance on each bill and let the title company settle it from proceeds. The buyer files the Property Transfer Affidavit with Assessing, and a seller who claimed the Principal Residence Exemption should ask Assessing how to end it. Cash buyers skip the lender's escrow step, which makes the payoff figure the main item to line up.

Frequently asked questions

What is the penalty if I pay my Troy summer bill late?

A 4% penalty is added on the first business day after September 1, and one-half of 1% monthly interest starts October 1. The winter bill carries a 3% penalty after February 14.

When does my Troy tax bill go to Oakland County?

On March 1, every unpaid current-year bill is transferred to the Oakland County Treasurer as delinquent, with added fees and interest. Pay the county at 1200 N Telegraph Rd, Dept 479, Pontiac, or call 248.858.0611, option 7.

Can I have a Troy payment taken from my bank automatically?

Yes, at no fee. Troy withdraws the payment on the due date, and a separate enrollment form is needed for property tax and for water and sewer. For the winter bill you choose February 14 or the last business day in December.

Who do I call in Troy about my home's value?

Call the Assessing Department at 248-524-3311. Office hours are Monday to Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., and appraiser visits can be booked for slots between 9:00 a.m. and 2:30 p.m.

How much time do Troy owners have to appeal a residential value?

The only window is the March Board of Review, and it applies to the current year. If you miss it, you give up the right to appeal that year's value.

Which city office handles your tax bill

Farmington Hills divides the work in two: the Treasury Division mails and collects the real and personal property tax, and the Assessing Division sets a value on every parcel. Both offices share a building at 31555 West Eleven Mile Road, Farmington Hills, MI 48336, and serve the public on weekdays between 8:30 and 4:30. The Treasury number is 248-871-2480 and Assessing answers at 248-871-2470.

The city lies in Oakland County. Whatever the city has not collected by early March moves to the county treasurer, and the city can no longer accept payment. The address for your check changes along with the cost of lateness.

How an assessment is set and challenged

The city aims for an assessed value equal to half of market value. Assessing studies 24 months of sales so that similar homes land in line, and each parcel is tied to a parcel number, a legal description and an address.

The State Tax Commission recommends reviewing roughly a fifth of properties each year, so an appraiser may stop by to look at your exterior. Notices of assessment go out every February, laying out the proposed valuation, the property class, principal residence exemption status, transfer status and appeal rights.

  • Read the February notice and the record card for errors in square footage, class or exemption status.
  • Call 248-871-2470 for an informal meeting with the assessor or staff before the March Board of Review.
  • Take a written appeal or an appointment request to the Board of Review in March.
  • Ask for copies of your records by phone or in person. Broader requests go through the City Clerk as a records request.

Balances still open on March 2 pass to the Oakland County Treasurer. Older years are already with the county, and checks go to the Oakland County Treasurer at 1200 N Telegraph Road, Pontiac, Michigan 48341-0479. Call the county at 248-858-0611.

A qualifying owner could defer the summer bill until February 16, 2027. Qualifying owners are at least 62, or totally and permanently disabled, blind, hemiplegic, paraplegic or quadriplegic, or an eligible serviceperson, veteran, widow or widower.

Assessing can answer questions about the homestead exemption, hardship or veteran's exemptions and taxable value. The city also links a list of state property tax assistance programs. Ask Treasury for the current year's form before summer bills go out, since the form is filed each year and the income limit can change.

Selling a house in Farmington Hills

Farmington Hills covers 33.31 square miles in Oakland County, bordered by West Bloomfield to the north, Franklin and Southfield to the east, Livonia to the south and Novi to the west. Almost all of the city is in Farmington Public Schools, and small portions are in Clarenceville and Walled Lake Consolidated. The main roads are M-5, Orchard Lake Road, 12 Mile Road, I-696 and I-275, with SMART buses serving the area.

An estimated 83,291 residents lived here as of July 2025, 0.9% fewer than the 2020 base. A typical owned home is valued at $354,500, and owners occupy 64.7% of housing. Households number 35,529 with a median income of $104,836, and renters pay a median of $1,551 a month. These are citywide medians, and individual blocks will differ.

What a seller owes at closing besides property tax

The state transfer tax, $3.75 per $500 of value under MCL 207.525, lands on the grantor under MCL 207.523. It is paid to the county treasurer inside 15 days of the deed being delivered.

A county transfer tax and recording fees come on top, and Oakland County's register sets its own charges. Before signing, ask the closing agent for a written statement showing the tax certificate, any open summer or winter balance and the recording costs.

A few steps help the closing go smoothly:

  1. Confirm that the summer bill and the winter bill are both paid or that the open balance is on the statement.
  2. If a balance has moved to Oakland County, call 248-858-0611 for a payoff.
  3. Tell Assessing about the sale so the next bill goes to the buyer.
  4. Keep your parcel ID handy, since every payment and certificate is tied to it.

A cash buyer can close without waiting on a lender, but the same tax certificate and payoff work still applies.

When is the winter tax bill due in Farmington Hills?

December 1 through February 16 without penalty. The bill is mailed November 30, and a 4% penalty is added on February 17.

Where do I pay old Farmington Hills taxes?

At the Oakland County Treasurer, not the city. Taxes from earlier years have been turned over to the county at 1200 N Telegraph Road in Pontiac, phone 248-858-0611.

Is there a fee to pay Farmington Hills property tax by card?

Yes. Card payments add 2.8% plus $0.50. Echecks have no fee, though a returned one costs $30.

How do I contest my Farmington Hills assessment?

Call Assessing at 248-871-2470 for an informal meeting, then use the March Board of Review, either by appointment or by letter received before the last meeting day.

Can seniors delay Farmington Hills summer taxes?

Possibly. The city's deferment form covers owners 62 or older, or disabled, blind or a qualifying veteran or surviving spouse, under a household income limit that was $40,000 on the 2026 form. Ask Treasury for the current form.

Who bills and who sets the value

The City of Southfield bills and collects its own property tax. Payments go to the Treasurer's Office in the City Hall Municipal Complex at 26000 Evergreen Road, where the counter is open weekdays from 8 a.m. until 5 p.m. Southfield sits in Oakland County, and the county treasurer takes over any balance the city has not collected once its own window closes.

A separate department sets values. Assessing counts every parcel as it stood on Tax Day, December 31, and aims each assessment at half of fair market value, using site visits, recorded transfers and a two-year sales study. Disputes about value are heard in March by the Board of Review.

Call the right line and you save a round of transfers. Treasurer, (248) 796-5200: due dates, payment methods, deferments, special assessments and millage. Assessing, (248) 796-5230: a value, a parcel number, an exemption or a new mailing address.

Due dates and penalties

Summer bills are payable July 1 through August 31 without penalty. Winter bills run December 1 to February 14. Each one is a payment window, so the last day of the window is your deadline.

Partial payments are accepted, and penalties and interest keep running on whatever is left.

Ways to pay a Southfield bill

Five routes exist, and the cost differs by route.

  • At the Treasurer's counter with a check, cash or money order.
  • By mail to the City of Southfield Treasurer's Office at the Evergreen Road address, with the parcel number written on the check and the envelope.

You can pay without the printed bill if you know the amount, as long as the check carries the parcel ID and your phone number. If a lender escrows your tax, the bill goes to the lender instead of you. When you pay on your own and no summer bill has shown up by July 1, ask the Treasurer for a copy. A missing bill does not stop the penalty clock.

What happens if the tax goes unpaid?

Once the city window closes, unpaid tax is handed to Oakland County and the cost climbs. Delinquent tax and earlier-year tax belong to the county treasurer in Pontiac, reachable at (248) 858-0611.

The county's fee is 4%, with 1% interest each month. Southfield's tax page also links a Delinquent Tax Timeline and a way to pay the county in cash at a 7-Eleven store. An owner who is behind and wants to sell should request a written payoff before choosing a closing date, because the number moves every month.

Exemptions and relief

Southfield offers three exemptions through Assessing and a deferment through the Treasurer. Each has its own form and proof requirements.

  • Principal Residence Exemption: owners who claim a house as their principal residence do not pay the school operating mills on the bill.
  • Hardship exemption: residents below the city's income guidelines may qualify. The application is on the Forms page under Assessment Resources.
  • Disabled veteran exemption: a VA disability rating of 100% or more, or a declared unemployable status, may qualify. The claim needs the annual VA Summary of Benefits letter, DD214, VA identification card and driver's license.
  • Summer tax deferment: for owner-residents with income up to $40,000 who are 62 or older, or retired because of a disability. Applications are taken only between July 1 and September 15.

Assessing takes real property transfers and exemption forms by email at contactassessing@cityofsouthfield.com, but every submission needs an original signature. Appointments with staff are booked through the Contact Staff page.

Selling a home in Southfield

Eight Mile Road forms the southern edge of Southfield, shared with Detroit, and Greenfield Road marks the east. The city of Lathrup Village sits as an enclave inside its eastern side. Office towers anchor the local economy, and Southfield City Centre sits where I-696 meets the Lodge Freeway (M-10). Southfield Public Schools runs a single high school, Southfield A&T, while the northern edge sends students to Birmingham schools and the southeast corner to Oak Park schools. Ask the title company to get a current tax status from the Treasurer before closing. The city's online inquiry system shows assessment and tax data free of charge. Confirm special assessments such as alarm billing or lawn mowing charges with the Treasurer, since a recent statement may leave them off.

Both sides then have paperwork. Assessing takes real property transfers and exemption forms, so ask which forms the buyer and the seller each owe for your parcel. A change of mailing address goes to Assessing in writing with the parcel number, a signature and the old and new addresses. No deed copy is required for a mailing change alone.

Nothing forces you to clear a balance before listing. Get the amount due on the parcel from the Treasurer and let the title company pay it out of your proceeds at closing. A buyer paying cash can close on a short timeline, and the same payoff step still applies, so request the figure early.

Frequently asked questions

When does Southfield summer tax become late?

Summer tax becomes late after August 31. Southfield adds 3.5% on September 1, then one-half of 1% on the first day of October and each month after that until the balance moves to Oakland County.

Which Southfield office do I call about my home's value?

Call the Assessing Department at (248) 796-5230 for values, parcel numbers and exemptions. Call the Treasurer's Office at (248) 796-5200 for bills, due dates and deferments.

Can Southfield give me more time to pay?

No extension is available for hardship or other reasons, because state law governs Michigan cities. Partial payments are taken, with penalties and interest on the rest. Seniors or disabled owners who qualify can apply for a summer deferment from July 1 to September 15.

Where does a Southfield bill go once the county has it?

Pay the Oakland County Treasurer in Pontiac, and call (248) 858-0611 for the amount. The county adds a 4% collection fee plus 1% interest a month.

How do I claim the Principal Residence Exemption on a Southfield house?

File the claim with the Southfield Assessing Department and sign it with an original signature. Approved owners do not pay the school operating mills portion of the tax bill.

The city collects for several bodies. Its own operating taxes are billed on the summer statement. The winter statement carries the county, school and authority levies, and Novi has no say over those rates.

Due dates and penalties

Novi bills in two seasons, late summer and winter. The city's 2026 notice said summer bills would be mailed the week of July 1 and had to reach the treasurer on or before August 31 to avoid an automatic penalty. Each year, expect the same rhythm: a summer bill with the city's own taxes, then a winter bill in December.

A drop box sits behind the Civic Center, and the city accepts drop box payments until midnight on deadline day. You can also pay by credit card or electronic check through cityofnovi.org. Double-check the bank numbers you type, because a returned payment after the due date draws the penalty.

How Novi sets the taxable value of a house

The bill rests on taxable value, a figure that normally sits below half of what the house would fetch. The assessor estimates market value as of Tax Day, December 31 of the year before, and the assessed value is about 50% of that. For 2026 the city used a 24-month sales study running from April 1, 2023 to March 31, 2025, covering roughly 2,000 sales.

Taxable value grows more slowly than assessed value. The 2026 inflation rate multiplier is 1.027, so a home that stays with its owner can rise no more than 2.7%, even if neighborhood prices climbed 10%. The city's formula is the prior taxable value, less losses, times the multiplier, plus additions.

  • Taxable value is the lesser of assessed value and capped value.
  • The tax equals taxable value divided by 1,000, times the millage rate.
  • A sale resets the taxable value to the assessed value the following year.
  • Special assessments, trash charges and penalties are added on top.

After you sell, the next owner's bill will probably run higher than yours did. Point any buyer to the assessed value rather than your old bill.

How to appeal your assessment

Appeals start with the March Board of Review, the only yearly chance to contest a current value. Hearings begin on the second Monday of March, after the Notice of Assessment goes out in mid February. Petition forms come from the Assessing Department or the city's website, and you make an appointment to appear.

If the board's answer is not acceptable, the next level is the Michigan Tax Tribunal. A residential petition must reach the Tribunal at 611 W. Ottawa St., Lansing, MI 48933 by July 31, and only after you have appeared before the March board. Commercial and industrial appeals to the Tribunal are due May 31. The July and December boards cannot hear value disputes under MCL 211.53b.

Two relief options sit outside the appeal process. Michigan has no age-based property tax break, but Novi offers an annual hardship exemption based on income and assets, which needs Board of Review approval. Owners who qualify can also ask the Treasurer's Office about deferring summer taxes.

Where a Novi tax bill goes

On the city's sample winter statement, about 59% of a homestead bill went to education, 30% to the City of Novi and 11% to Oakland County. That split used the Novi and OCC district homestead rates, so a parcel in another district will differ. Several school systems reach into the city.

  • Novi Community Schools cover most of the city.
  • Northville Public Schools serve a large part of the south side.
  • Walled Lake Consolidated Schools take in a pocket with two elementary schools.
  • South Lyon Community Schools hold a small western strip.

Other lines on the statement include the county parks and recreation levy, the zoo authority, the art institute, Oakland transit and the Huron Clinton Metropolitan Authority. Check the parcel number and school district code on your own bill before you compare it with a neighbor's.

When Novi taxes go unpaid

After the winter period closes, the balance moves to Oakland County. Under MCL 211.78a, taxes still owed on March 1 become delinquent, with a 4% county fee and interest at 1% for each month. The county treasurer collects from there, and continued nonpayment leads into a three-year foreclosure process.

For 2024 and earlier balances, March 31, 2027 is the final day to pay and keep the property. The county treasurer's office, at 248-858-0611, offers repayment schedules and referrals. Our Oakland County property tax guide lays out the foreclosure calendar step by step.
